fig_growth.webp.summary: The number of studies (economic evaluations and reviews of them) has grown rapidly. Half of the included research was published from 2020 onwards. The 2026 count covers only part of the year.

fig_method_stream_v2.svg.title: How studies measure health benefits is changing
fig_method_stream_v2.svg.summary: More studies now use measures that combine length and quality of life. These measures help compare health benefits across different diseases. Reviews that report no evaluation of their own are shown separately and not counted as an evaluation type. The 2026 count is incomplete and left out.

fig_disease_circular.webp.title: Which diseases does the economic evidence focus on?
fig_disease_circular.webp.summary: This chart shows which disease groups, as defined by the Global Burden of Disease study, receive the most research attention, and whether that research leans toward richer or poorer countries. A study can cover several groups, so the percentages can add up to more than 100%. Only studies that name a disease are included.

fig_transition.webp.summary: Research about lower-income countries has moved from infections and maternal and child health towards non-communicable diseases, broadly in step with the changing disease burden; research on injuries stays well below their share of the burden.
fig_transition.webp.title: Research in lower-income countries is shifting towards long-term illnesses

paper04.webp.title: Disease priorities are changing in lower-income countries
paper04.webp.summary: Compare the diseases studied in earlier and later years. In research about lower-income countries, HIV/AIDS & STIs and maternal & neonatal account for a smaller share, while cancers (neoplasms) account for more. Studies can cover several disease groups.
paper04.webp.caption: Disease mix of studies by period (2010–17, 2018–26) and income group. Infectious disease is falling as a share of low- and middle-income research while cancer and respiratory disease rise; the high-income mix is comparatively flat. Disease areas from MeSH subject headings; bars are 95% confidence intervals and point size shows the number of studies.

paper05.webp.title: The diseases studied differ by country income
paper05.webp.summary: Malaria, HIV/AIDS and other infections feature more often in research about lower-income countries. Cancer and heart disease feature more often in higher-income settings. A study can appear in more than one disease group.

fig_intervention_map.webp.title: What kinds of healthcare does the research cover?
fig_intervention_map.webp.summary: Each dot is a study, placed near studies with similar summaries. Colours show the type of health care studied. Dot positions are not places on a map.
fig_intervention_map.webp.caption: A two-dimensional map of all the studies, built by grouping their abstracts by similarity (73 clusters). Panel A colours each study by its main intervention type, labelled with that type's share of studies about low- and middle-income countries (LMICs); panel B colours the same map by that share. Vaccines (41% LMIC) and financing/payment policy (32%) lean most towards LMICs; devices (17%) and care models (23%, with surgery close behind at 23%) lean most towards high-income countries; pharmaceuticals (30%) sit just above the 27% overall share. Base: 27,930 single-country studies with a known income group. Intervention types were assigned by a large language model from each abstract (main type only).

fig_theme_rank.webp.title: Research topics differ between higher- and lower-income countries
fig_theme_rank.webp.summary: Compare the topics most concentrated in higher-income settings with those most concentrated in lower-income settings. These are the two ends of the topic range, rather than a list of the most commonly studied topics overall.

fig_intervention_mix.webp.title: What gets evaluated: types of healthcare by country income
fig_intervention_mix.webp.summary: Compare the share of studies evaluating medicines, vaccines, surgery and other types of healthcare. Each study is counted under its main intervention. The chart includes studies about one country with known income.

paper01.webp.title: How records were selected for the evidence map
paper01.webp.summary: The map includes 41,657 studies, including 1,706 reviews of earlier studies. The diagram shows how records were screened and selected.
paper01.webp.caption: Study selection (PRISMA flow): 72,845 records reached data extraction; 41,657 were included as full economic evaluations — 39,951 articles reporting their own evaluation and 1,706 reviews of published evaluations. Reviews were kept by design and are counted separately; most (67%) name no single country, so country-level figures draw mainly on articles.

fig_metric.webp.title: How health benefits are measured differs by country income
fig_metric.webp.summary: Studies use measures of healthy life gained or illness avoided. A QALY combines length and quality of life; a DALY measures healthy life lost to illness or early death. A study may report either, both or neither.

paper02.webp.title: Studies using models more often report measures that compare health benefits across diseases
paper02.webp.summary: Compare studies that estimate costs and outcomes with a model and studies that measure them in patients. The chart shows how often they report QALYs or DALYs, which help compare health benefits across diseases.

fig_intervention_decision.webp.title: What studies report to help healthcare decisions
fig_intervention_decision.webp.summary: Compare reporting across types of healthcare. The chart checks for information about value for money, uncertainty and whose costs are considered. It uses what is reported in abstracts, so a missing item does not mean the study did not address it.

fig_dotmap.svg.summary: Each bubble represents a country; larger bubbles mean more studies mention it. Colours show country income. A study covering several countries can appear in several bubbles.
fig_dotmap.svg.title: Most economic evidence is about high-income countries

fig_worldmap.webp.summary: This map compares the number of studies examining each country with that country's population. A country is counted when a study examines it, not where the authors are based; a study examining several countries counts for each. It shows research coverage rather than the quality of the evidence or the amount of funding received.
fig_worldmap.webp.title: Studies examining each country, per person
fig_worldmap.webp.caption:
Per-capita choropleth (Robinson): studies naming each country per 10
                      million people. Mid-grey = the 54 countries and territories named by no
                      eligible study (of 241 Natural Earth polygons, Antarctica excluded); pale grey
                      = named but outside the 155-country list the shading uses. 31,775
                      study–country pairs across 187 countries.

paper03.webp.title: How much research is available relative to population?
paper03.webp.summary: Compare the number of studies examining each country per 10 million people, across country income groups. Countries are those the studies examine, not where the authors are based. This adjusts for population size, but does not measure research quality or whether enough evidence exists.

fig_authorship_pattern_v2.svg.title: Are local researchers involved in studies about their countries?
fig_authorship_pattern_v2.svg.summary: Compare studies with authors based in the country studied and studies involving authors based elsewhere. A third of studies about low-income countries have no author based there. Author location comes from recorded institutional affiliations, which are known for 85% of studies.

fig_forest_v2.svg.title: Local authorship differs across regions
fig_forest_v2.svg.summary: Most studies about a country include an author based there, but this happens less often in Africa (WHO region), at about three in four studies. Author location comes from recorded affiliations and does not establish who led the study.

paper06_v2.svg.title: Some studies about lower-income countries have no locally based author
paper06_v2.svg.summary: A third of studies about low-income countries have no author with a recorded affiliation there. Missing or incomplete affiliations can affect this estimate; local authorship does not necessarily mean local leadership.

fig_collab_chord_v2.svg.title: How researchers collaborate across country income groups
fig_collab_chord_v2.svg.summary: The connections show studies whose authors are based in different income groups. Almost all of these collaborations include an author based in a high-income country, while most studies have authors from only one income group. Recorded affiliations identify author locations, rather than funding or study leadership.

fig_research_burden_ratio.svg.summary: Each dot is a country. Dots below the line have less research than their share of the world's illness and early death would suggest. A typical low-income country has about a tenth of that share; a typical high-income country has about twice its share. The line is a reference point, not a target.
fig_research_burden_ratio.svg.caption: Base: 154 countries with disease-burden data; 31,471 study–country counts (a study naming several countries counts once for each). Eritrea and Mauritius have no identified studies. Studies published 2010–2026 (final year partial); disease burden is GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs. Ratios compare shares, so countries well above the line push others below it. The line is a reference point, not a measure of adequacy. Horizontal position within a group is spread out only for readability.

paper07.webp.summary: Compare how many studies examine each country relative to that country's illness and early death. The comparison adjusts for disease burden, but does not determine how much research a country needs.
paper07.webp.caption: Studies per 100,000 DALYs (healthy years lost) against total disease burden, by country and income group (2023). The typical high-income country has 22 times as many studies per unit of burden as the typical low-income country. Studies naming each country divided by GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs; point size shows population.

fig_burden_disease_companion.webp.title: Does research attention match the burden of different diseases?
fig_burden_disease_companion.webp.summary: Compare each disease group's share of research with its share of illness and early death, in lower-income and high-income countries. This helps identify areas receiving relatively less research attention.

paper08.webp.title: Some disease groups receive less research attention relative to their burden
paper08.webp.summary: Injuries, especially self-harm, violence and road injuries, and mental disorders show the largest differences between research attention and disease burden. The comparison is a reference point, not a target.
paper08.webp.caption: Research share divided by disease-burden share for 13 of the 14 disease areas (Other NCD, a residual group, is left out), by income group: points left of 1 have a smaller share of research than of burden. Injuries and, in poorer settings, mental & substance use show the largest gaps; maternal & neonatal is also a gap in low- and middle-income settings (about 0.7×) while high-income research runs about 5× its burden share. Disease areas from MeSH subject headings; burden from GBD 2023 DALYs.

fig_deficit.webp.title: Where are the largest differences between research and disease burden?
fig_deficit.webp.summary: This chart highlights the largest differences between the number of studies examining each country and that country's disease burden.
fig_deficit.webp.caption: Base: all 204 national GBD 2023 locations, including zero-study locations; 31,627 unique study–country pairs. Expected studies = this pair total × the country's share of DALYs across the same 204 locations. Hong Kong, Cayman Islands, French Guiana and Guadeloupe have no row in the national GBD export and their pairs are excluded. Bars show the 16 largest deficits and 8 largest surpluses. This larger country set differs from the 154-country website burden analysis (31,471 pairs). Country colours use July 2026 income groups. Studies published 2010–2026, final year partial; GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs. Proportionality is a reference point.

fig_injustice.webp.title: How research attention compares with disease burden worldwide
fig_injustice.webp.summary: Compare where research is concentrated with where illness and early death occur. Equal shares provide a reference for comparison, rather than a target for research or funding.

fig_inequality.webp.title: How research coverage varies with disease burden
fig_inequality.webp.summary: Compare the amount of research available with the level of illness and early death. A low study count does not by itself show whether the evidence is sufficient or useful.
fig_inequality.webp.caption: Base: 106 LMIC countries with GBD 2023 all-cause DALYs; 8,732 study–country pairs; 2 countries have no study. Countries ordered by studies per DALY. The first 41 countries crossing 50% of burden carry 53.9% of burden and 1,455 pairs (16.7%); the marker is at these actual coordinates. The five countries with the greatest burden (India, China, Nigeria, Indonesia, Pakistan) instead carry 51.7% of burden and 48.1% of evidence. Gini = 0.49. Country grouping uses July 2026 income classifications; studies span 2010–2026, final year partial. Each multi-country study counts once per country.

fig_openaccess.webp.summary: More studies are available to read without paying. The chart uses recorded open-access status; unknown access status is not treated as paywalled.
fig_openaccess.webp.caption: Share of studies that are open access, by year and by the income of the country studied (2010–25; 2026 partial, left out). Fewer than half were open in 2010; by 2025 about four in five were. All three lines use single-country studies with a known income group and a known open-access status: 22,970 studies. Open-access status is from OpenAlex and is known for about 87% of studies.

fig_funder_funders.svg.title: Top funders: who funds economic evidence, and where?
fig_funder_funders.svg.summary: The bars show how many studies report each funder, rather than how much money they provided. Only about 27% of studies report a funder in the dataset, so this is an incomplete picture. Colours show the income group of the country studied; grey retains other settings and missing income information.

fig_map_burden.webp.title: Where is research more or less abundant relative to disease burden?
fig_map_burden.webp.summary: This map compares research coverage with illness and early death. It shows relative research attention, rather than whether a country has enough evidence or should receive a particular funding amount.

fig_map_openaccess.webp.title: Where is evidence available to read for free?
fig_map_openaccess.webp.summary: Compare recorded open-access availability across countries. Access information is incomplete; an unknown status does not necessarily mean an article requires payment.

fig_map_growth.webp.summary: Compare how the number of studies examining each country has grown. Growth describes publication counts rather than evidence quality. The final publication year is incomplete.

fig_map_authorship_v2.svg.title: Where do studies include locally based authors?
fig_map_authorship_v2.svg.summary: This chart shows, for each WHO region, how often studies include an author based in the country studied. It uses recorded affiliations, which can be incomplete, and does not establish who led the research.

fig_map_model.webp.title: Where do studies estimate outcomes with models or measure them in patients?
fig_map_model.webp.summary: Compare studies using models to estimate costs and health outcomes with those drawing on measured patient outcomes. This describes their approach, rather than judging their quality.
fig_map_model.webp.caption: Share of each UN sub-region's studies that estimate results with a decision model rather than measure them in a study, against the global average (63.9%, dashed). This average counts each study once for every country it names, so it differs from the 54% on the Overview. Latin America and the Caribbean relies on models most (78.8%), Southern Asia least (57.4%). Base: 30,633 study–country pairs (sub-regions with fewer than 100 left out).

fig_equity_time.webp.title: A growing share of research focuses on lower-income countries
fig_equity_time.webp.summary: Track the share of studies about low- and middle-income countries over time. Publication counts show research attention, rather than funding amounts or evidence quality.

fig_reach_time.webp.title: More countries now have at least one study
fig_reach_time.webp.summary: Track how many countries are mentioned in at least one included study. Having one study indicates some coverage; it does not mean there is enough evidence for all healthcare decisions.
fig_reach_time.webp.caption: Cumulative reach through each publication year. Countries are grouped by the World Bank classification in force on 1 January of that year; the denominator excludes unavailable country-year groups. Taiwan uses the recorded high-income override. A country is reached once any eligible study has named it by that year, including studies from its earlier income groups. In 2025, solid lines cover 154 classified countries from the 155-country website list (2 unreached); dashed lines cover 197 classified/overridden Natural Earth Sovereign country/Country entities (21 unreached), with no population floor. Denominators vary by year; 197 is not a fixed count of all World Bank economies. 2026 is partial and omitted, so the Ethiopia/Venezuela 2026 fallback does not affect these lines.

fig_decision_time_v2.svg.title: Studies increasingly report information that helps assess value for money
fig_decision_time_v2.svg.summary: Track how often abstracts mention costs relative to health benefits, uncertainty and other information useful for decisions. These are abstract-based checks; an item may be addressed in the full paper even if it is absent from the abstract. Reviews that report no evaluation of their own are left out.

fig_funder_opportunity.webp.title: Evidence gaps: where is research scarce relative to health needs?
fig_funder_opportunity.webp.summary: Explore disease groups and income levels with relatively little evidence compared with disease burden. These comparisons help identify questions for further investigation; they do not estimate the cost or benefit of new research.

fig_funder_scorecard_v2.svg.title: Evidence gaps: where is research coverage lowest relative to disease burden?
fig_funder_scorecard_v2.svg.summary: Compare the share of studies examining each country with that country's share of global disease burden. A study examining several countries counts for each. Because the comparison uses shares, large countries do not dominate the ranking. Ratios based on few studies are less stable.

fig_funder_capacity.webp.title: Local capacity: where could research capacity be strengthened?
fig_funder_capacity.webp.summary: Compare indicators of local research participation and evidence coverage. These signals can guide further investigation, but do not directly measure skills, infrastructure or the cost of building research capacity.

fig_funder_trajectory.webp.title: Gap trends: which evidence gaps are narrowing over time?
fig_funder_trajectory.webp.summary: Compare changes in research coverage over time. Past publication trends show what has happened, rather than predicting future research or funding needs.

fig_wellcome_priorities.svg.title: Wellcome-funded studies: which priority themes do they cover?
fig_wellcome_priorities.svg.summary: This chart counts studies that report Wellcome Trust as a funder in each theme, with Wellcome's share of theme studies and its rank among reported funders. The grey bar shows studies outside all three themes. Disease groups provide broad theme indicators, and Climate & Health uses a reviewed title-and-abstract screen. Climate & Health is small because few studies in the map address climate. Themes can overlap; these counts are not a complete record of Wellcome grants.

wellcome_analysis.html.summary: Explore the evidence and recorded funders within Wellcome's priority themes. The view separates all theme-related studies from Wellcome-funded studies. Theme coverage and funding records are incomplete. Climate & Health is a reviewed title-and-abstract screen, and is small because few studies in the map address climate.

fig_glance_regions_who_v4.html.title: Health Economic Evaluations
fig_glance_regions_who_v4.html.summary: Headline figures for the evidence map, then where full economic evaluations are concentrated relative to disease burden, by country and by WHO region: each region's disease focus, top diseases, use of utility measures (QALYs, DALYs) and country coverage over time. Use the information buttons to see how each measure was calculated.

fig_glance_regions_who_v3.html.title: Research coverage and health needs by region
fig_glance_regions_who_v3.html.summary: Compare WHO regions' research coverage against disease burden, with headline figures and each region's disease focus, use of utility measures (QALYs, DALYs) and country coverage over time. Use the information buttons to see how each measure was calculated.
